entry.title: Deep Dive into Delta Lake
entry.content:
History

As you might already know, the creators of Apache Spark founded Databricks, and initially used Spark along with Apache Hive Metastore for their big data processing. However, as I have discussed in my previous post, Apache Hive tracked files strictly at folder/partition level and if you needed to make an update to a single row, you’d have to swap out and rewrite the entire folder. This means it was highly inefficient for writes, and if a write failed halfway through, it would leave partially written files behind that readers would treat as valid data. Furthermore, Spark pipelines running on cloud object storage like Amazon S3 lacked ACID properties, which led to data corruption and partially written data folders when processing jobs crashed.

To solve this problem, Databricks built Delta Lake around 2017, which introduced a centralised transaction log (_delta_log). It was open-sourced in April 2019 and later that year moved to the Linux Foundation.

A Quick Recap

Delta Lake is among the three most popular and most used Open Table Formats (OTFs) used in production today. Like other OTFs, Delta Lake provides ACID compliance, Schema Evolution, Data Versioning, and reduces vendor lock-in.

Architecture

Note: The _delta_log file names in the diagram are shortened for readability. Actual commit files are zero-padded to 20 digits (e.g., 00000000000000000000.json).

Let’s start from the beginning, you land/dump your raw data into an object storage (like S3).

Using a processing engine, primarily Apache Spark, you write the data out directly as Delta format, which consists of standard Apache Parquet files (a highly compressed, columnar format):

df.write.format("delta").save("s3://my-bucket/delta-table")

The moment an engine executes this command, it first writes the Parquet data files and then creates a _delta_log/ folder with a commit that lists them. If the job crashes before the commit, readers never see those files. This directory is now a Delta Table.

Every time an engine makes changes to this table, Delta Lake makes an entry in the _delta_log/ using sequential, numbered JSON text files (e.g., 00000000000000000000.json, 00000000000000000001.json, 00000000000000000002.json). Each of these entries is called a commit and states exactly which files were added or removed, along with any schema changes.

A commit only succeeds if the writer is the first one to create the next numbered JSON file. If two writers try to create the same file at the same time, one wins. If the changes don’t conflict, the other writer retries; if they do, it fails. This is how Delta Lake makes sure that concurrent writes don’t step on each other. On S3, writing from multiple clusters historically needed a DynamoDB-backed log store, because S3 couldn’t guarantee that only one writer creates a file.

When a query engine wants to read the data, it reads these JSON files first to figure out which Parquet files are the latest and valid. Because the number of commits can grow tremendously over time, reading hundreds of JSON files from start to finish would eventually become slow. To prevent this, after every 10 commits, Delta Lake automatically creates a checkpoint Parquet file (e.g., 00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet), which captures the full state of the table at that point. A reader can then start from the latest checkpoint and only read the few JSON commits after it.

Performance

There are a lot of optimizations you can do in terms of reads and writes with Delta Lake, some of the important ones are:

Z-Ordering

Delta Lake colocates rows with similar values in the chosen columns in the same files. Since Delta Lake stores the min/max values of the first 32 columns (by default) for every file in its _delta_log, the engine can skip the files that can’t match your WHERE clause, reducing the amount of data scanned and speeding up queries.

Delta Lake doesn’t automatically guess which data is related. Instead, you would analyse your most frequent query WHERE clauses and explicitly run an OPTIMIZE command:

OPTIMIZE my_delta_table ZORDER BY (customer_id, country)

Delta Lake then uses a mathematical concept called Space-Filling Curve (specifically a Morton Curve / Z-Order curve), where it takes the binary representations of the values in those columns and zips them together like a deck of cards to create a single number (Z-value) for each row, and it then sorts the data by this new Z-value before writing the rows into Parquet.

Challenges with Z-Ordering

  • Curse of Dimensionality: Z-ordering works well with 2 or 3 columns, but it breaks down when you try to order 5 or 6 columns. If you intertwine two decks of cards (Columns A and B), the pattern is a tight A B A B A B…. But if you intertwine 5 columns, the pattern stretches out to A B C D E A B C D E…. This stretches the rows that share the same value for Column A wildly far apart across files, diluting the sorting effectiveness for each column.
  • Query Pattern Changes: If your business needs change and you need to filter by a brand new column, you have to redo the Z-ordering process from scratch across your historical data.
  • High Write/Compute Costs: Because Z-ordering requires a full sort and isn’t incremental, running it forces your Spark cluster to read, shuffle, and rewrite massive amounts of data from scratch, resulting in heavy compute bills.

Liquid Clustering: The Successor to Z-Ordering

Liquid Clustering replaces the rigid bit-math of Z-Ordering with a fluid spatial clustering algorithm (built on Hilbert curves). When new data arrives, Liquid Clustering doesn’t sort the whole historical table. Instead, it writes the new data quickly into separate files in your object storage. When you trigger an OPTIMIZE command, it uses the Hilbert curve algorithm to cluster only the data that isn’t clustered yet, leaving the already clustered files alone. This makes ordering significantly faster and cheaper. Because of the spatial curve design, it can cluster by up to 4 columns with better data skipping than Z-ordering on the same columns.

And if your query patterns change, you can simply change the clustering columns without rewriting your existing data:

ALTER TABLE my_delta_table CLUSTER BY (customer_id, order_date)

The existing data keeps its old clustering until later OPTIMIZE runs re-cluster it with the new columns.

Liquid Clustering replaces both partitioning and Z-Ordering, so it can’t be combined with either of them. It started on Databricks and is now available in open-source Delta Lake 3.x.

Compaction of Files

In streaming or high-frequency batch workloads, data is often written into S3 in small, fragmented files. This causes massive metadata read overhead. Query engines perform far better on fewer, larger files, and Delta Lake has a default target file size of 1 GB for OPTIMIZE (which is fully adjustable; on Databricks it is tuned automatically based on table size).

To fix this, you run an OPTIMIZE command (without ZORDER):

OPTIMIZE my_delta_table

Delta Lake reads its transaction log to check for Parquet data files that are significantly smaller than the target size. The Spark engine reads these tiny files into cluster memory, brings them together logically, and merges them into one or more files of around 1 GB. Delta Lake then writes a new JSON file to the _delta_log/ to commit this update, marking the old small files as removed.

Limitations

  • Storage Bloat: Because Delta Lake guarantees ACID compliance and Time Travel, it never deletes or overwrites an old file during a compaction or an update. It simply flags it as removed in the log. This causes massive file accumulation and storage bloat in your S3 bucket, meaning you must regularly monitor and run a VACUUM command to physically purge old files. By default, VACUUM keeps files from the last 7 days, and once old files are purged, you can no longer time travel to the versions that used them.
  • Tied to Databricks and Spark: As Delta Lake is tightly woven and heavily optimized for Databricks and Spark runtimes, non-Spark engines like Presto, Trino and Amazon Athena historically struggled to read Delta tables natively, requiring external symlink manifest files to understand which Parquet files were active. Today, Trino and Amazon Athena can read Delta tables natively. Delta Lake has also introduced Universal Format (UniForm), which writes Iceberg metadata alongside the Delta log so other engines can read Delta tables as if they were Apache Iceberg tables. But these engines only get read access, and you still need a catalog like Unity Catalog to expose that metadata, adding to architectural complexity.
entry.summary: History, architecture, performance optimizations and limitations of Delta Lake

entry.title: Evolution of Data Storage Layers
entry.content:
In the Data Engineering Lifecycle, Data Storage Layer spans across all the other layers and hence is a backbone of your entire data architecture. And the data can be stored anywhere from databases, data warehouses, data lakes. But how these systems handle data is vastly different and the storage option you select depends on the business use case and how the downstream app consumes them.

Databases

This is one of the most familiar topics and hence we will not go into depth. As we know, for different needs we have different databases. Some of the most popular ones are Relational databases (Postgres, MySQL, Amazon Aurora), Document DBs, Wide-Column DBs, Graph DBs, and Key-Value DBs, etc. Storing data into these DBs is primarily for OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) purposes. They do not serve well for analytical workloads (OLAP) such as calculating trends or aggregations across millions of records. Because the data in these transactional databases is mostly stored in rows on the disk, the engine is forced to scan a massive amount of unnecessary data just to extract and compute a single metric, taking significantly more time than the specialized analytical options we’ll see below.

Data Warehouse

A Data Warehouse is an excellent option for analytical workloads. This is where you dump all of your structured data that has been generated from sources such as:

  • Transactional Systems: Relational databases like PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Amazon Aurora.
  • SaaS Applications: Structured data exported from tools like Salesforce, HubSpot, or Stripe.
  • Logging Systems: Application or system logs that follow a strict, predefined schema.

Because it stores structured data and enforces schema-on-write, it is ideal for downstream systems like BI tools for report generation and dashboarding.

Under the hood, data warehouses use columnar storage. While traditional databases read data row-by-row (making them slow for analytical calculations), data warehouses store data column-by-column. If a dashboard only needs to calculate total revenue, the engine skips all other columns on the disk and reads only the revenue data, making analytics extremely fast.

However, there are challenges with Data Warehouses:

  • Rigid Structure: Data must be structured into rows and columns before entry. Modern warehouses can handle semi-structured JSON (e.g., Snowflake VARIANT, Redshift SUPER, BigQuery JSON), but they cannot natively store raw, unstructured data like videos, audio, or images.
  • The Ingestion Bottleneck: Transforming and cleaning massive volumes of high-velocity, real-time data before writing it to the warehouse can easily lag or bottleneck your data pipeline.
  • Loss of Granular History: Because data must be aggregated or transformed to fit the warehouse schema, you often need to throw away the original, raw data that a data scientist or ML engineer might need for machine learning years down the line. However, sometimes companies might not throw away the raw data but instead store it somewhere, this maintenance of data at multiple places creates complexity.

Data Lake

Because of the above challenges of Data Warehouses, Data Lakes were invented. Data Lakes act as a centralised repository and let you store data in its raw, native format without needing to structure it first unlike Data Warehouses, as they follow schema-on-read. They are very cheap and separate storage from compute, letting any engine read the data. They are also extremely flexible in the types of data that can be stored:

  • Structured Data: Tabular rows and columns.
  • Semi-Structured Data: JSON payloads, XML files, and CSVs.
  • Unstructured Data: PDFs, text documents, emails, videos, and audio recordings.

Despite their flexibility, Data Lakes are bad for traditional business reporting and dashboarding, as they are not indexed and don’t follow ACID compliance and the reporting/dashboarding requires fast, clean SQL tables.

This meant companies needed to maintain 2 types of data storage systems for analytics. Data warehouses with structured data for reporting/dashboarding and data lakes with all types of data for Machine Learning. Maintaining this is expensive, time consuming and operationally painful. Data Engineers will need to constantly write complex pipelines to sync and move data back and forth between these storage systems. And as I mentioned above, Data Lakes don’t comply with ACID, concurrent writers could corrupt data mid-write and there was no dependable way to know which files represented a table’s current, accurate state.

Data Lakehouse

Because of the need to maintain 2 different storage systems, Data Lakehouse was born. To oversimplify it, it is a mix between a Data Warehouse and a Data Lake, meaning you can store all kinds and types of information into your Data Lakehouse, and it will have a magic metadata layer that turns the files in your lake into reliable tables to let you query them with SQL for reporting, all while preserving the raw data underneath for Data Science & ML.

Magic Metadata Layer

Spoiler alert, there is no magic here. In reality, a Data Lakehouse adds a metadata layer, called an Open Table Format, on top of columnar files (such as Parquet) in the lake. Raw semi-structured data is first parsed into columns by an engine like Spark, and the Open Table Format then tracks exactly which files make up a table at any point in time. This is what gives plain files on object storage warehouse-like guarantees: ACID transactions, time travel, and schema evolution. Unstructured data like videos and PDFs stays raw in the lake. It gets the name “Open” because the table specifications are completely public i.e., any query engine can read them without being locked into a single proprietary database vendor.

While there are three popular open table formats used in production today, they all keep a metadata layer that records which data files belong to the table (a file-level index that maps out where data lives). However, how they organize and manage this metadata under the hood is different:

  • Apache Iceberg: Organizes metadata in a hierarchical, tree-based structure (Metadata File -> Manifest Lists -> Manifest Files), with column statistics stored in the manifests so engines can skip unneeded files without opening them.
  • Delta Lake: Open-sourced by Databricks, it uses a transaction log approach (_delta_log/, an ordered ledger of JSON commits with periodic Parquet checkpoints) to track table history and updates.
  • Apache Hudi: Originally created by Uber, it uses a timeline (.hoodie/) of actions on the table and specializes in streaming workloads and low-latency incremental updates, organizing files to handle rapid upserts and deletes.

Side Note: Before the above table formats, the industry relied heavily on Apache Hive tables. Hive mapped a table name to a directory in the Data Lake and applied a schema to the files at read time. Because Hive didn’t track data at a file-level but rather at a folder-level (whatever files were in the folder were the table), if we needed to update a single row in a file, we would need to re-write the whole folder (partition) again. Hive 3 did later add ACID tables, but in practice most data lakes used plain, non-ACID Hive tables. Think of it like a folder containing 50 physical pages of text. If you want to change just one sentence on Page 42, Hive forces you to modify Page 42 and then re-write all 50 pages completely from scratch because it treats the folder as an inseparable bundle.

In contrast, modern open table formats use their metadata layer to provide file-level tracking. Data files are immutable and never edited in place, so if you need to make a change on Page 42, the engine writes a new version of only that 1 page (Page 42) and commits it atomically. Because the metadata already lists every file in the table, engines also no longer need to slowly list folders to find the data. Under the hood, this precision is handled using one of two concepts:

Copy-on-Write

The engine takes the original page_42_v1, reads it into memory, applies your update, and writes a brand-new page_42_v2 to your storage bucket. The old file is left completely untouched, and the commit creates a new snapshot of the table that references page_42_v2. The previous snapshot still references page_42_v1, which is what makes time travel possible.

Merge-on-Read

Instead of rewriting any major data files, this method keeps the original page_42_v1 completely as it is. It writes a separate, lightweight file containing only the specific delta (the update/delete action), such as delete files in Iceberg, deletion vectors in Delta Lake, or log files in Hudi. When you query or read the data through an engine like Apache Spark or Amazon Athena, the engine pulls both the old file and the tiny delta file simultaneously, merging them in memory on the fly to show you the updated data. The trade-off is that writes become fast but reads get slower as delta files pile up, so a periodic compaction job folds them back into the data files.
entry.summary: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Data Lakehouse
